title: Surgeons’ risk judgments diverge from forest-model estimates
summary: Thirty-nine spine surgeons estimated complication and reoperation risks for nine adult-spinal-deformity case vignettes. Their judgments varied widely and had low agreement with estimates from an existing random-survival-forest calculator. This measured disagreement does not show that the calculator was more accurate for these cases: actual patient outcomes were not the comparator. A 39% response rate, selected vignettes and inconsistent directional wording in the paper limit interpretation.
organization: Vall d’Hebron University Hospital; European Spine Study Group; International Spine Study Group

source_review.scope: Primary Duke author-deposited journal PDF front matter, relevant calculator/survey Methods, Results/Tables1–3 and discussion/limitations. Publisher canonical identity and journal online date corroborated. Exact primary identity/date and fresh primary PubMed correction/retraction relationships checked.

evidence.tested: Comparison of 39 surgeons’ elicited risk estimates for nine fixed case vignettes against an existing random-survival-forest calculator. Mean indices of agreement with the model ranged .122–.416 across complication/reintervention endpoints and follow-up horizons.
evidence.unknown: Accuracy versus actual outcomes, improved counseling and patient benefit were not established by this comparison. Group-average differences were not statistically significant; low individual agreement should not be recast as proven machine superiority. One Results sentence reverses the temporal direction shown in tables and discussion, so directional over/underestimation claims are omitted.
evidence.ai_role: A previously trained random survival forest generates case-specific risk estimates that provide the learned comparator for measuring agreement with human judgments.
